issues.issue: Article I applies the agreement only to excess policies written "excess of underlying insurance which afford limits not less than" the Schedule of Underlying Limits, yet Article III (Retention and Reinsurance) expressly contemplates that the underlying Hospital Professional Liability limit may be "self-insured" rather than insured. Whether a self-insured retention or a state compensation fund satisfies Article I's underlying-insurance requirement cannot be answered from Article I alone.

The enumerated coverage list (Commercial General Liability, Hospital Professional Liability, Automobile Liability, Non-Owned Aircraft and Heliport Liability) has no catch-all, so an excess policy insuring some other hospital-related exposure falls outside the cession. The scope of "the REINSURED'S excess liability policies" is defined only by that closed list.

The Schedule requires $5,000,000 underlying Heliport Liability, while Article II(c) excludes loss arising out of the ownership, operation or use of helicopters owned or leased by the insured hospital. The two cannot easily both be given effect for a hospital with its own helicopter service.

The clause deems a discovery period or extended reporting endorsement part of the original policy period "subject to the provision that a separete Limit of liability may apply in respect thereof," without saying who decides or when a separate limit applies. The permissive "may apply" leaves the reinsurer's exposure for a tail period indeterminate.

The clause incorporates "The Nuciear Incident Exclusion Clauses and the Insolvency Clause" as attached, but the attached Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 2 refers to a "Broad Exclusion Provision" whose text does not appear anywhere in the instrument. What is incorporated is therefore incomplete on the face of the agreement.

Exclusion (a) turns on whether the insured operates a "teaching hospital, childrenst hospital or psychiatric hospital," none of which is defined; a general hospital with residency programs or a pediatric unit may or may not qualify. The exclusion gives no test for how much teaching or pediatric activity makes a hospital one of the named kinds.

Exclusions (a), (b) and (d) of this Article were deleted and replaced by Amendment No. 1 for policies becoming effective on or after July 1, 1995, so which version of the exclusion governs a given ceded policy depends on reading the two together. The original 250-bed and children's/psychiatric hospital exclusions cannot stand with the substituted 350-bed, teaching-hospital-only text.

The article's 90%/10% split applies only where "the underlying Hospital Professional Liability limit of $1,000,000/$3,000,000 is self-insured," a term the agreement nowhere defines. Whether coverage through a captive, a state patients' compensation fund, or a retention endorsement counts as self-insured decides who bears the first $1,000,000.

"Loss" is confined to amounts "within applicable policy limits as are actually paid by the REINSURED in settlement of claims or in Satisfaction of awards or judgments," which does not say whether sums paid in compromise of disputed or arguably uncovered claims qualify. The 90% sublimits in (b) and (c) further leave unclear how a single settlement is allocated between ordinary loss and extra-contractual loss.

"Net salvage, subrogation or any other recovery (after expenses)" does not identify which expenses are deducted or how recoveries are shared where loss straddles the retention. The catch-all "any other recovery" has no stated boundary.

"Claim expenses" is defined by reference to "the supplementary payments provisions of the REINSURED'S policy," a provision an umbrella or excess form may not contain, and then by a list ending in "ailocated investigation, adjustment, and legal expenses." Whether unallocated or in-house defense costs fall inside the definition is left open.

The exclusion of "salaries paid to employees of the REINSURED" sits against the definition of claim expenses in the preceding paragraph, which includes "allocated investigation, adjustment, and legal expenses." Time charged by the reinsured's own staff adjusters or in-house counsel is caught by both provisions at once.

The proviso allocates claim expenses "connected with such settlement or appeal" although the sentence introducing it speaks only of a verdict, award or judgment reduced or reversed on appeal, never of a settlement. The mismatch leaves unclear whether appellate-stage settlements are covered by the ratio rule or by the general pro rata rule.

The article fixes premium by "the Rating Schedule, attached hereto," but that schedule was deleted and replaced by Rating Schedule-A (Amendment No. 1) and again by Rating Schedule-B (Amendment No. 4). Which schedule the unamended article points to for a given policy year must be worked out from the amendments.

The operative contingent-commission promise is unreadable in the executed text, and Amendment No. 1 deleted this first paragraph of Article VII and substituted a 40%-of-net-profit formula limited to the first $1,000,000 of reinsured limits. What obligation this paragraph imposes can only be determined by reference to Amendment No. 1.

The accounting-period mechanism is internally inconsistent: periods are said to commence "on January Ist of every ether year" and run twenty-four months, yet a final period on early termination is said to commence "on the fifth January 1st preceding the termination date." A twenty-four-month cycle and a five-year lookback cannot both be right.

This paragraph directs that if any computation shows a net profit the CORPORATION "shall pay to the REINSURED the full contingent commission," while the later paragraph of Article VII forbids payment of further contingent commission until all premium is earned and all losses paid. The two payment triggers conflict.

The Accounting Schedule credits list is mechanically broken: only item "1." is numbered and the salvage credit is left unnumbered, yet the charges list refers back to "Item i of Credits to Profits." Which item the 15% overhead charge is measured against turns on numbering the text does not supply.

The charge "a sum for home office overhead equal to 15% of Item i of Credits to Profits" identifies its base only by an item number that the garbled credits list does not clearly assign. The list's own numbering ("iL. 4a.") is unusable for identifying the four charges.

"Unpaid losses" is to be calculated "on the reserve of individual cases," without saying whose reserve — the REINSURED's case reserves or the CORPORATION's — controls. Since reserves drive the contingent-commission charge, the ambiguity is consequential.

The deficit carry-forward rule must be read with the computation paragraph of Article VII, which promises "the full contingent commission" whenever a computation shows a net profit. Whether a prior deficit is charged again in every later annual recomputation or only once is not settled by either provision alone.

"Net profit" is defined as the excess of credits over charges under the agreement-wide Accounting Schedule, but Amendment No. 1 limits contingent commission to "the first $1,000,000 of reinsured limits as respects each policy." How an agreement-wide profit figure is restricted to a per-policy first-million layer is not addressed in either text.

This paragraph bars any further contingent commission until all premium is earned and all losses paid, which cannot be squared with the earlier Article VII paragraph requiring payment of the full contingent commission whenever a computation shows a net profit. Which rule governs post-termination accounting periods is left to construction.

The bordereau must be "on a form satisfactory to the CORPORATION," a standard left wholly to the reinsurer's judgment and with no stated content requirement. Whether a cession is properly reported — and thus reinsured — turns on that undefined satisfaction.

The duty to remit "the amount due the CORPORATION" within 20 days must be read with the Offset article (Article XII), which lets either party set off balances under this or any other agreement between them. Whether remittance is gross or net of offsettable balances is not stated here.

The REINSURED must give "prompt notice" of "any event on development which might result in a claim upon the CORPORATION," neither of which is defined or tied to a fixed period. What triggers the notice duty for an excess layer, and how late is too late, is the classic construction question this wording invites.

The right to participate arises for claims to which, "in the judgment of the CORPORATION, it is or might become exposed," a self-referential standard with no objective boundary. The scope of the reinsurer's associate-in-defense right is therefore indeterminate.

Reimbursement is due "promptly" upon receipt of "satisfactory evidence of payment of such loss," with neither the time nor the sufficiency of proof defined. Whose satisfaction governs, and what proof suffices, are left open.

The advance-funding sentence is garbled and self-contradictory as written: the CORPORATION is to "furnish to the REINSURED the CORPORATION'S Payment of loess" on the date the REINSURED proposes to pay, while the preceding paragraph makes reimbursement contingent on evidence of payment already made. Whether pre-payment funding is an enforceable obligation is unclear.

The inspection right extends to records "pertaining to the risks reinsured hereunder," with no limit on time, place, or the reinsured's privileged or claims-file material. The scope of "pertaining to" is the whole of the boundary.

The offset right extends to balances under "any other reinsurance agreement heretofore ox hereafter entered into" between the parties, which sits uneasily with the Insolvency Clause's requirement that reinsurance be paid without diminution to the liquidator. Whether cross-agreement offset survives insolvency is not resolved by either provision.

The article permits termination only by mutual consent or 90 days' registered-mail notice, yet the Stipulation of Termination terminated the agreement prospectively as to "policies issued on or after January 1, 1998" without reference to either mechanism. How the Stipulation operates under this article requires reading the two together.

In-force policies run off "but in no event exceeding i2 months plus odd time," and "odd time" is nowhere defined in the agreement. The outer limit of the reinsurer's post-termination exposure depends on that undefined phrase.

Discovery period and extended reporting endorsements attaching to policies "in force prior to or as ef the effective date im time of cancellation" remain covered, but the phrase does not say whether tails purchased after the termination date are included. Read with Article I's clause treating tails as part of the policy period with a possibly separate limit, the extent of run-off cover is uncertain.

This nuclear pool exclusion duplicates Article II(e), which already excludes the REINSURED's liability as participant or member of any pool of insurers formed for specific coverages. Whether the two exclusions have the same reach, or the narrower nuclear clause qualifies the broader article, is a question of reading them together.

Nuclear Incident Exclusion Clause No. 4 is expressly a "(Physical Damage)" clause excluding insurance against physical damage, yet Article I confines this agreement to enumerated liability coverages. The clause has no evident field of operation in a liability-only cession.

The carve-out from paragraph (3) turns on whether "a REINSURED does nat have knowledge" of the nuclear installation, with no time or diligence standard for that knowledge. Whether constructive knowledge defeats the exception is unaddressed.

The paragraph excludes radioactive contamination only when it is "a named Nazarea specifically imsaired against," a phrase whose intended meaning (a named hazard specifically insured against) is recoverable only by correcting the text. As printed the exclusion's trigger is unreadable.

The clause does not extend to risks where the nuclear exposure "is not considered by the REINSURED to be the primary hazard," making the exclusion's reach turn on the ceding company's own subjective view. No objective test of "primary hazard" is supplied.

Making the REINSURED "sole judge" of what constitutes substantial quantities and the extent of an installation hands the ceding company control over the scope of an exclusion the reinsurer wrote. Read with paragraph (2), which turns on "substantial Quantities of racdicactve isatopes," the exclusion is effectively unilateral.

The transition provision grandfathers policies issued on or before 31 December 1957, which can have no application to an agreement whose Effective Date is January 1, 1994. The clause is inoperative dead text within an instrument that incorporates it as a part.

The Canadian-risk transition provision grandfathers policies issued on or before 31 December 1958, which cannot operate under an agreement effective January 1, 1994 and applying to Ohio-area hospital risks. Its inclusion leaves an incorporated term with no possible field of operation.

The paragraph deems original policies to include a "Limited Exclusion Provision" "fron the time specified io Clause (71 an this paragraph (2)," but no such clause is legible or present in the attached text. The date from which the deemed exclusion operates cannot be determined from the words used.

This paragraph deems listed liability policies to include the "Broad Exclusion Provision" from the time specified in "Clause V of this paragraph," but neither the Broad Exclusion Provision nor Clause V appears anywhere in the agreement as attached. The exclusion it purports to import has no text in the instrument.

The insolvency payment obligation is carved out by "Section 4118 of the Insurance Law of New York," a statute with no evident application to an agreement between a Kansas reinsurer and an Ohio ceding company. What the exception excepts, and under what state's law, is left open.

The liquidator must give notice of a pending claim "within a reasonable time after such claim is filed," an unquantified standard, while Article IX requires "prompt notice" of any event that might result in a claim. Which standard binds a statutory successor is not stated.

Defense expense is chargeable against the insolvent ceding insurer only "to the extent of a proportionate share of the benefit which may accrue," with no method for measuring that benefit. The proportion is left entirely to later argument.
